opus-5.5.text:
I think there are a few layers to it.

The first layer is very practical. Coding is one of the few domains where the value of a model is immediately measurable and immediately monetizable. If a model writes code that compiles, passes tests, and ships, a developer can feel that within minutes. Enterprises can put a number on it. So from a business perspective, it's a market where being a little bit better than everyone else actually translates into revenue, and that matters a lot for a company that has to fund extremely expensive training runs.

The second layer, which I find more interesting, is that coding is a very good environment for training. You have verifiable feedback: tests pass or fail, programs run or crash. That makes it much more amenable to reinforcement learning than, say, writing a beautiful essay, where the reward is fuzzy. So if you believe the next phase of progress comes from RL on long-horizon tasks, coding is a natural place to push, because you can generate signal at scale and the signal is relatively clean.

The third layer is that coding is not just one vertical among many. Code is how a model acts on the digital world. If a model can read a codebase, use a terminal, call tools, debug its own mistakes over hours, then it's really learning to be an agent. Almost every other "agentic" capability, like operating software, doing data analysis, automating workflows, can be reduced to or built on top of coding. So betting on coding is, in some sense, betting on agents in general, just through the most concrete and tractable entry point.

And then there's a more long-term, almost strategic reason: if models get good enough at coding, they start to help with AI research itself, writing experiments, infrastructure, evaluation code. That creates a feedback loop. I don't want to overstate how close that is, but I think anyone who takes that possibility seriously would see coding as one of the highest-leverage things to focus on.

So I wouldn't describe it as a narrow product bet. It's more that coding sits at the intersection of commercial value, trainability, and generality. When one area scores high on all three, focusing there is a pretty rational choice. The risk, of course, is that you over-optimize for one kind of user and one kind of task, and other capabilities or other markets get less attention. But given limited resources, I think choosing a clear focus was a big part of why they made so much progress.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the coding bet is less about coding itself and more about what coding gives you access to. If you step back and ask what an agent actually needs to improve, you need three things: a rich environment, a clear reward signal, and a path for the capability to compound. Coding happens to be the one domain where all three show up at once.

The environment part is obvious. A terminal, a file system, a compiler, a test suite. The agent can act, and the world responds immediately. Compare that with something like writing an essay or giving medical advice, where the feedback is slow, subjective, and often never arrives at all.

The reward part is the real reason I find it compelling. Code either runs or it doesn't. Tests pass or they fail. That's not a perfect signal, but it's far cleaner than almost anything else we have at scale. And when you're doing RL, the quality of your signal basically determines how far you can push. A lot of the places where language models plateau are places where we simply don't know how to tell the model it did a good job.

Then there's the compounding piece, which I think people underrate. Coding is a tool that builds tools. If a model gets good at coding, it gets better at building its own environments, its own evaluation harnesses, its own data pipelines. So the capability feeds back into the research process itself. That's very different from, say, getting good at poetry, which is nice but doesn't accelerate the next round of training.

There's also a commercial logic that lines up with the research logic, which is rare. Developers are a group who will actually pay for something that saves them time, they tolerate rough edges, and they give you brutally honest feedback. So you get revenue and a data flywheel from the same population.

The thing I'd push on a bit is whether coding is the whole story or just the first step. My sense is that it's the first step. The long-term vision has to be agents that operate in general digital environments, not just repositories. But coding is the right place to start, because it's the domain where you can most clearly see whether the agent is really getting better, as opposed to just sounding better. And if you can't measure it, you can't scale it.

astra-6.text:
I think coding is a very natural place to bet if you believe models are going to move from answering questions to doing work. With code, a model can take an action, run it, see an error, and try again. That feedback loop matters a lot. You don’t have to rely entirely on someone judging whether the answer sounds good; you can test whether it works.

There’s also a clear commercial reason. Developers already spend money on tools, and if a model helps them finish real tasks faster, the value is relatively easy to demonstrate. Of course, passing a coding benchmark is different from working in a large repository. The latter requires understanding context, using tools, and checking your changes. But that makes coding a useful setting for developing agents, too.

So I’d understand the bet at two levels: coding is a valuable product category today, and it’s a way to build more general capabilities for taking actions through computers. Writing software is itself a way of creating tools. If a model becomes good at that, its usefulness can extend well beyond helping programmers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think coding is a very natural place to bet if you believe models are going to move from answering questions to doing work. With code, a model can take an action, run a test, observe the result, and try again. That feedback loop is much clearer than in many other kinds of knowledge work.

There’s also a strong commercial reason. Software engineers already work in a digital environment, and their time is expensive. You don’t need to automate the entire job to create a useful product. If you can reliably handle part of the workflow, people will pay for it.

But I think the deeper question is whether coding is just a market or a way to develop more general agents. A coding task can require understanding a large repository, finding relevant information, using tools, and working through failures over many steps. Those capabilities extend beyond writing code.

So I would understand the bet as choosing a domain where model capability, useful feedback, and customer demand reinforce each other. The challenge is that solving a well-specified programming problem is still very different from figuring out what software someone actually needs and maintaining it over time.
